documents: Li et al. 2022, JGR Solid Earth 127, e2022JB024719, published PDF (17 pages); Supporting Information not supplied
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 17), which equal PDF pages counted from 1

entry.evidence: Few investigations, however, have taken advantage of passive seismic sources to continuously monitor the reservoir response to CO2 injection

steps.action: The authors pose the aim: characterize high-frequency (1–20 Hz) noise near the CO2 injection well and relate it to injection activity, using noise migration and PSD.
steps.quote: we examine the high-frequency noise (1–20 Hz) near the CO2 injection well using continuous data from a dense geophone array

steps.action: They use continuous three-component 10 Hz geophone records from a dense square array and two trench lines (May–June 2019) and from an X-shaped 19-station array (August 2019), sampled at 250 Hz.
steps.quote: continuous three-component seismic data were recorded using three dense surface arrays of 10 Hz geophones

steps.action: They design the test around two known anthropogenic sources (the injection well and a submersible water disposal pump) as ground truth for locating sources.
steps.quote: We use these noise sources as ground truth for our independent investigation of seismic sources.

steps.action: They compute day-stacked noise cross-correlations: 30-s windows with 50% overlap, downsampled to 40 Hz, instrument response removed, spectrally whitened, then stacked.
steps.quote: we adopt a preprocessing workflow similar to the method described by Bensen et al. (2007) and Lin et al. (2013)

steps.action: Cross-correlation record sections along the two diagonal lines show asymmetric arrivals at 0.2–0.5 km/s, which establishes that persistent local noise sources are non-uniform and directional (southeast, and west of line 2).
steps.quote: suggesting directionally dependent noise source distributions

steps.action: They exclude active shot sources such as vibroseis because the signals are weak and last hours rather than seconds.
steps.quote: These sources are unlikely to correspond to active shot sources such as a vibroseis truck

steps.action: They build a modified grid-search migration of normalized correlation envelopes (50 m cells, 300 m/s straight-ray surface-wave velocity taken from correlation moveout and prior FRS work) and a PSD/PDF workflow on 30-min segments in 1/8-octave and 1-dB bins.
steps.quote: We adopt a grid-search migration algorithm based on stacked noise-correlation amplitudes

steps.action: They migrate the 1 June 2019 vertical-vertical correlations in four frequency bands and locate a dominant 1–5 Hz (and 15–20 Hz) source in the southeast and a weaker 5–15 Hz source at the array center.
steps.quote: Two prominent noise sources are detected in the study area

steps.action: They compare the located sources with the known infrastructure: the southeastern source coincides with the water disposal pump and the central source with the injection well.
steps.quote: the noise source from the southeast of the array coincides with the operation of subsurface water disposal

steps.action: They repeat the migration on the N–N and E–E horizontal components (supplement Figures S3–S4). The results are generally consistent but more diffuse, so they keep the vertical component only.
steps.quote: only vertical-vertical components are used in our noise source migration analysis due to the higher spatial resolution

steps.action: They compare daily near-well and whole-array migration amplitudes (30 May–23 June) with the five injection days. Injection is only slightly concurrent with higher noise, and the southeastern source dominates at 1–5 Hz.
steps.quote: The injection activity is slightly concurrent with an increase in noise level.

steps.action: They attribute the 1–5 Hz southeastern signal to water pump operation, citing H/V work, and suggest mechanical pump vibration for the 15–20 Hz signal.
steps.quote: we suspect that the mechanical vibration from the water pump is a probable candidate for generating the high-frequency signal

steps.action: Synthetic control (supplement Text S1, Figures S5–S7, Table S1): they place explosive sources at the well and the pump, add 0–20% Gaussian noise, process with the same workflow, and recover the source locations.
steps.quote: we adopt a forward modeling approach by comparing our noise migration results with those reconstructed based on synthetic seismograms

steps.action: They vary the assumed migration velocity (supplement Text S2, Figures S8–S13); the same two sources appear.
steps.quote: we conduct a sensitivity test of assumed migration velocities and examine the robustness of the noise migration results

steps.action: Independent method: they compute station PSD/PDFs against the NLNM/NHNM references and map the peak mean PSD across the array. High noise at the southeast station F0901 and at the center agree with the migration maps.
steps.quote: To further verify our findings, PSDs were calculated from individual records to understand the characteristics of cultural noise.

steps.action: They average PSDs over near-well, southeast-corner and background subregions. Both source regions are noisier than the background, show a 10–30 dB day-night difference, and the pump region is steady below 10 Hz.
steps.quote: To assess the diurnal variations of the two observed noise sources, we divide the study area into three subregions

steps.action: Replication with the August 2019 sparse X array, using both migration and PSD. The southeastern source repeats; the central source is less robust and more diffuse, but its spectral power is higher than in June.
steps.quote: we further investigate noise characterization from continuous data recorded by a surface array in an “X” configuration

steps.action: They compute hourly PSD time series and PDFs at F0405, the geophone nearest the well, for June and August.
steps.quote: we calculate the time series of PSD values for geophone F0405, the nearest receiver to the injection well

steps.action: They compare the F0405 spectra with injection times and with two known field projects (a deviation survey and a field school). The injection association is clearer in August, and the field school is visible in late-August spectra.
steps.quote: the association between CO2 injection activity and noise level is more apparent in August 2019 (yellow arrows)

steps.action: They attribute the night-time drop in noise to reduced vehicle and truck traffic, and the late-August peaks to field-school activity.
steps.quote: The reduced off-road vehicles or truck traffic likely contributes to the observed drop in noise level during nighttime.

steps.action: They note that the center source drifts east in the daily maxima (supplement Figures S13–S14) and that noise amplitude correlates only weakly with injection mass, given the discontinuous injection.
steps.quote: the noise amplitude results show a weak correlation with the injection mass

steps.action: They draw on the group's earlier results: no seismicity at the FRS, implying no overpressure at the low injection rate, and a noise-seismicity relation linked to aseismic deformation in central Alberta.
steps.quote: the absence of seismic activity within the injection zone at the FRS (Savard et al., 2019, 2020) indicates the injection is unlikely to create overpressure

steps.action: They propose that the central source is microtremors from CO2 fluid-rock coupling (stress redistribution, aseismic or rock deformation, fluid movement), while stating that temperature, precipitation, groundwater and nonstationary ambient sources cannot be excluded.
steps.quote: we propose that the persistent noise source around the injection well is probably derived from the persistent microtremors

steps.action: They keep the two-source finding and the CO2 fluid-rock microtremor interpretation as preliminary evidence, and propose the method for long-term storage monitoring.
steps.quote: Our analysis provides preliminary evidence for persistent noise sources around the injection well

tree.answer: Persistent non-ambient local noise sources around a CO2 injection site, established from asymmetric correlations
No; source locations are inferred by migrating noise correlations and mapping PSDs
Locate and characterize noise sources and relate them to injection and to pump activity
Pump, injection, vehicles/field work and vibroseis; for the center source, fluid-rock interaction versus temperature, precipitation, groundwater and nonstationary ambient noise
Not derived for the mechanism rivals; the synthetic test only checks that source locations are recovered
Conditions found during live operations (injection days, pump, field projects); none were set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Injection days repeat in June and August; the correlation with injection mass is weak
Southeast source survives components, velocity, PSD and the August array; the center source weakens in the sparse array
Two sources kept; the CO2 fluid-rock microtremor origin is proposed as preliminary

end.claim: Two persistent local noise sources are present at the FRS: a 1–5 Hz southeastern source tied to water disposal, and a 5–15 Hz source at the injection well, which the authors propose comes from microtremors of CO2 fluid-rock interaction.

decisive_move.sentence: The grid-search migration of noise-correlation envelopes that located a distinct 5–15 Hz source at the injection well is the step without which there would be no claim about an injection-related source.

gates.evidence: The data come from the FRS passive monitoring deployments, not from an acquisition designed to test the hypothesis. The source locations faced tests they could have failed: the synthetic control, the velocity sensitivity test, the PSD maps and the August array. The fluid-rock mechanism faced no discriminating test, since rivals 'cannot be excluded' (p. 13). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen, although the known sources were declared as ground truth (p. 3).

imports.item: Image similarity measures (mutual information, structural similarity) used to compare synthetic and observed migration maps (supplement Table S1; references from the Supporting Information)
Pump and mechanical vibration literature used to explain the 15–20 Hz signal near the pump

novelty_claims.quote: as well as the low cost of our method together, provide new possibilities for long-term monitoring of CO2 sequestration.
Although the spectral content of the noise generated by this water pump has not yet been studied due to the lack [...]

limits: No review file or Supporting Information was supplied, so the checks reported only in the supplement (horizontal components, synthetic test, velocity sensitivity, eastward drift) are coded from main-text descriptions. Sub-claim statuses: the source locations are estimate_with_resolution, though no spatial resolution or uncertainty is quantified; the link of the southeastern source to the pump is best_explanation; the method's monitoring capability is at most partly capability_characterized. The injection-noise relation is described qualitatively and is called weak (p. 13); no statistical test is reported. The diurnal pattern (higher noise in daylight working hours) could also reflect human site activity; this is inference, as the paper partly attributes it to traffic. The rival mechanisms for the center source are listed but not tested. There are internal inconsistencies: recording dates are given as May–June, June, and 30 May–23/24 June; the text reports AMA >0.85 at 1–5 Hz while the Figure 4 colorbar tops at 0.78 (inference from the figure); and Figures 6 and 11 are cited for the correlation with injection mass although they are PSD panels. Raw data are not public; only the cross-correlations are shared. Proposed future work (3D migration, depth resolution) was not done here.

disagreements.target: Conventional active-source (controlled source 3D/4D) seismic monitoring prioritized by most CO2 storage projects
disagreements.support: The paper argues on cost, logistics and periodic sampling, and offers passive noise monitoring as a cheaper continuous alternative, without a direct performance comparison.
disagreements.quote: The drawbacks of this approach are its high cost and extensive logistic effort.

disagreements.target: Locating sources by phase or body-wave picking (as in microseismicity detection, Savard et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: The authors assert that picking is difficult for these weak persistent sources and use picking-free migration instead; no comparison is shown.
disagreements.quote: it is challenging and inaccurate to locate the noise source based on picking body wave arrivals in a small-time window

alternatives_considered.chosen: Grid-search migration of stacked noise-correlation amplitudes
alternatives_considered.alternatives: beamforming, matched field processing, cross-correlation inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: does not require travel time picking
higher spatial resolution; horizontal results noisier and more diffuse

alternatives_considered.alternatives: other assumed migration velocities in the sensitivity test; ~325 m/s from previous FRS studies
alternatives_considered.reason: corresponds roughly to the maximum energy in the correlation functions and is similar to prior FRS results

alternatives_considered.chosen: Keep remote earthquake signals in the PSD time series
alternatives_considered.reason: they occupy short intervals and lie below 1 Hz, outside the cultural noise band

alternatives_considered.chosen: PDFs built from all available PSDs
alternatives_considered.alternatives: preprocessing to select a quiet period (Peterson, 1993)
alternatives_considered.reason: evaluates the full range of noise without needing quiet-period selection
picking in a small time window is challenging and inaccurate
